patterns.name: Basic SELECT and filtering
patterns.problem: List rows/columns that satisfy simple conditions.
patterns.template:
SELECT `Company`, `City`
FROM customers
WHERE `State/Province` = 'WA'
  AND `City` <> 'Seattle';
patterns.explanation: WHERE filters rows before any grouping. Quote identifiers that contain spaces or "/" with backticks; string literals use single quotes.
mistakes: Using double quotes for strings (MySQL may read them as identifiers in ANSI mode).
Forgetting backticks around `Last Name`.
Using = NULL instead of IS NULL.
notWhen: When the condition needs an aggregate: use HAVING.

patterns.name: ORDER BY and LIMIT
patterns.problem: Sort the result and keep only the first rows.
patterns.template:
SELECT *
FROM products
ORDER BY `List Price` DESC, ID
LIMIT 5;
patterns.explanation: ORDER BY sorts, LIMIT cuts after sorting. Add a tie-breaker column so the output is deterministic.
mistakes: LIMIT without ORDER BY gives arbitrary rows.
Ties at the cut-off are silently dropped.
Writing ORDER BY a DESC, b when both must be DESC.
notWhen: When ties must all be returned: use a subquery on the threshold value or RANK()/DENSE_RANK().

patterns.name: DISTINCT / unique values
patterns.problem: Return each value only once.
patterns.template:
SELECT DISTINCT `Ship Country/Region`
FROM orders;
patterns.explanation: DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows (whole row, not first column). COUNT(DISTINCT x) counts different values of x.
mistakes: Believing DISTINCT applies to only the first selected column.
Using DISTINCT to hide a wrong join that multiplies rows.
COUNT(DISTINCT a, b) is not the same as two separate counts.
notWhen: When per-group aggregates are also needed: use GROUP BY.

patterns.name: Aggregate functions
patterns.problem: COUNT / SUM / AVG / MIN / MAX over a set of rows.
patterns.explanation: Aggregates collapse rows into one value; NULLs are ignored by every aggregate except COUNT(*).
mistakes: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col): the latter skips NULLs.
AVG over a column with NULLs ignores them (not treated as 0).
Mixing non-aggregated columns without GROUP BY.
notWhen: When a value per group is needed: add GROUP BY.

patterns.name: GROUP BY and HAVING
patterns.problem: Aggregate per group and filter on the aggregate.
patterns.template:
SELECT `Customer ID`, COUNT(*) AS n_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY `Customer ID`
HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;
patterns.explanation: GROUP BY forms groups; HAVING filters groups after aggregation (WHERE filters rows before). More than N => > N, at least N => >= N.
mistakes: Putting an aggregate in WHERE.
> vs >= (more than vs at least).
Grouping by a name that is not unique (group by the ID too).
Selecting columns that are not in GROUP BY.
notWhen: When filtering on a plain column: use WHERE (cheaper).

patterns.name: INNER JOIN
patterns.problem: Combine rows from related tables; only matching rows survive.
patterns.explanation: JOIN ... ON links the foreign key to the primary key. Rows without a partner are dropped.
mistakes: Missing ON clause (cartesian product).
Joining on the wrong key (the dump declares no FK constraints).
Fan-out: joining one-to-many then summing a parent column.
notWhen: When unmatched rows must be kept: LEFT JOIN.

patterns.name: LEFT JOIN (keep unmatched)
patterns.problem: Keep all rows of the left table even without a match.
patterns.template:
SELECT c.ID, c.`Company`, COUNT(o.`Order ID`) AS n_orders
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.`Customer ID` = c.ID
GROUP BY c.ID, c.`Company`;
patterns.explanation: Unmatched left rows get NULLs on the right. COUNT(right.key) gives 0 for them; COUNT(*) would give 1.
mistakes: Filtering the right table in WHERE turns the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN (put the condition in ON).
COUNT(*) instead of COUNT(right.col).
notWhen: When only matching rows are wanted: INNER JOIN.

patterns.name: Subquery (scalar / derived table)
patterns.problem: Use the result of one query inside another.
patterns.explanation: A scalar subquery returns one value; a derived table in FROM needs an alias.
mistakes: Scalar subquery returning more than one row (error).
Missing alias on derived table.
notWhen: When it can be a plain join without losing clarity.

patterns.name: EXISTS
patterns.problem: Keep rows for which a related row exists.
patterns.explanation: EXISTS stops at the first match and is NULL-safe; no duplicates from the outer table.
mistakes: Forgetting the correlation condition (EXISTS always true).
notWhen: When you need columns from the inner table: JOIN.

patterns.name: NOT EXISTS / anti-join
patterns.problem: Keep rows with NO related row.
patterns.explanation: NOT EXISTS is the safe anti-join. Equivalent: LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL.
mistakes: NOT IN with a subquery that returns NULL gives an empty result.
Inner join + <> does NOT express "never".

patterns.name: IN / NOT IN
patterns.problem: Membership test against a list or subquery.
patterns.explanation: IN tests against a set. NOT IN is dangerous when the set contains NULL (comparison becomes UNKNOWN for every row).
mistakes: NOT IN + NULL in subquery => no rows.
Large IN-lists are slow compared with a join.
notWhen: Negation with nullable columns: use NOT EXISTS.

patterns.name: Correlated subquery
patterns.problem: Inner query references the outer row.
patterns.explanation: The inner query runs per outer row (logically). Typical for "greater than the average of its own group".
mistakes: Using the same alias in both levels.
Forgetting the correlation => global average.
notWhen: Big tables: a window function or a join to a grouped derived table is usually faster.

patterns.name: SELF JOIN
patterns.problem: Join a table to itself to compare rows or form pairs.
patterns.template:
SELECT a.`Product ID` AS p1, b.`Product ID` AS p2, COUNT(*) AS together
FROM `order details` AS a
JOIN `order details` AS b ON a.`Order ID` = b.`Order ID` AND a.`Product ID` < b.`Product ID`
GROUP BY a.`Product ID`, b.`Product ID`
ORDER BY together DESC;
patterns.explanation: Two aliases of one table. Use < (not <>) on the key so each unordered pair appears once and no row pairs with itself.
mistakes: <> returns each pair twice.
Missing the self-pair exclusion.

patterns.name: Conditional aggregation
patterns.problem: Several filtered aggregates in one pass (pivot-like).
patterns.template:
SELECT `Employee ID`,
       SUM(CASE WHEN `Shipped Date` IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS not_shipped,
       SUM(CASE WHEN `Shipped Date` IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS shipped
FROM orders
GROUP BY `Employee ID`;
patterns.explanation: SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN x ELSE 0 END) or COUNT(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 END) counts/sums only matching rows per group.
mistakes: COUNT(CASE ... ELSE 0 END) counts every row (0 is not NULL).
Using WHERE would filter away the other categories.

patterns.name: Date manipulation
patterns.problem: Filter or group by year/month/day.
patterns.template:
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(`Order Date`, '%Y-%m') AS ym, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM orders
WHERE `Order Date` >= '2006-01-01' AND `Order Date` < '2007-01-01'
GROUP BY ym;
patterns.explanation: Prefer a half-open range (>= start AND < next start) over YEAR(col)=2006: it can use an index. DATE_FORMAT builds YYYY-MM keys.
mistakes: BETWEEN with datetime misses the last day after 00:00:00.
Functions on the column disable index use.
Mixing %m (month) and %i (minute) in DATE_FORMAT.

patterns.name: Ranking and Top-N (incl. Nth)
patterns.problem: Top N rows, Nth highest, ranking with or without ties.
patterns.template:
SELECT *
FROM orders
ORDER BY `Shipping Fee` DESC, `Order ID`
LIMIT 3 OFFSET 5;  -- 6th..8th row

-- ties-aware: DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY `Shipping Fee` DESC) BETWEEN 6 AND 8
patterns.explanation: LIMIT/OFFSET ranks by ROW position; RANK/DENSE_RANK rank by VALUE and treat equal values as tied. Decide which one the question means.
mistakes: OFFSET is 0-based: 6th row => OFFSET 5.
Ignoring ties.
Nth highest value vs Nth row.

patterns.name: Multiple-table aggregation
patterns.problem: Join several tables then aggregate.
patterns.template:
SELECT c.ID, c.`Company`, SUM(od.`Unit Price` * od.Quantity) AS total
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o ON o.`Customer ID` = c.ID
JOIN `order details` AS od ON od.`Order ID` = o.`Order ID`
GROUP BY c.ID, c.`Company`;
patterns.explanation: Follow the key chain customers -> orders -> order details -> products. Aggregate at the end, group by the entity key.
mistakes: Summing an orders column after joining order details (fan-out, double counting).
Grouping by name only.

patterns.name: Query optimization
patterns.problem: Make a query use indexes and read less data.
patterns.explanation: Avoid SELECT *, avoid functions on indexed columns, filter early, index filter/join/sort columns, check with EXPLAIN.
mistakes: Index on a column wrapped in a function is unused.
Leading-wildcard LIKE is not index-friendly.

patterns.name: NULL handling
patterns.problem: Missing values in filters, aggregates and comparisons.
patterns.explanation: NULL = anything is UNKNOWN. Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, COALESCE for defaults; aggregates skip NULLs.
mistakes: col = NULL never matches.
<> excludes NULL rows silently.
NOT IN with NULL.

patterns.name: Relational division
patterns.problem: Entities related to ALL members of a set.
patterns.template:
SELECT o.`Customer ID`
FROM orders AS o
JOIN `order details` AS od ON od.`Order ID` = o.`Order ID`
JOIN products AS p ON p.ID = od.`Product ID`
WHERE p.Category = 'Beverages'
GROUP BY o.`Customer ID`
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT p.ID) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products WHERE Category = 'Beverages');
patterns.explanation: Count the distinct members each entity covers and compare with the total number of members. Alternative: double NOT EXISTS.
mistakes: COUNT without DISTINCT.
Comparing against a count that was not restricted to the same subset.

patterns.name: Computed columns and ratios
patterns.problem: Derived expressions, ratios, rounding, percentages.
patterns.explanation: Column aliases cannot be used in WHERE; repeat the expression or use HAVING / a derived table. 50% => 0.5.
mistakes: Alias in WHERE.
Percent written as 50 instead of 0.5.
Division by zero yields NULL in MySQL.

patterns.name: ALL / ANY comparison
patterns.problem: Compare with every / at least one value of a subquery.
patterns.template:
SELECT * FROM products
WHERE `List Price` > ALL (SELECT `List Price` FROM products WHERE Category = 'Beverages');
patterns.explanation: > ALL = greater than the maximum; > ANY = greater than the minimum. Equivalent to comparing with MAX()/MIN().
mistakes: Mixing up ALL and ANY.
ALL over an empty set is true.

patterns.name: UNION / UNION ALL
patterns.problem: Stack results of several queries.
patterns.explanation: UNION removes duplicates (extra sort/dedup); UNION ALL keeps all rows and is faster. Column counts and types must match.
mistakes: UNION when duplicates are wanted.
Different column order between branches.

patterns.name: String functions
patterns.problem: Build or split text: CONCAT, UPPER, REPLACE, SUBSTRING_INDEX, LIKE.
patterns.template:
SELECT CONCAT(`First Name`, ' ', UPPER(`Last Name`)) AS full_name,
       SUBSTRING_INDEX(`E-mail Address`, '@', -1) AS domain,
       REPLACE(`Job Title`, 'Sales ', '') AS short_title
FROM employees;
patterns.explanation: CONCAT returns NULL if any argument is NULL (CONCAT_WS skips NULLs). SUBSTRING_INDEX(s, sep, n): n>0 text before the nth separator, n<0 text after the nth separator from the right. LENGTH counts bytes, CHAR_LENGTH counts characters.
mistakes: Forgetting the space/trailing separator in REPLACE.
LENGTH vs CHAR_LENGTH.
LIKE wildcards: % any string, _ one character.

entries.sourceRef: SQL_Mock_Test_2025.docx Q1 (1 pt)
entries.question: Return the list of customers (Last Name, First Name, Job Title), sort them by Last Name, then First Name, both by descending order.
entries.explanation: Each sort key needs its own DESC: `ORDER BY a DESC, b` sorts b ascending. Identifiers with spaces need backticks.
mistakes: `ORDER BY `Last Name`, `First Name` DESC` (DESC applies only to the last key).
Forgetting backticks around `Last Name`.
Sorting by the select position of the wrong column.

entries.sourceRef: SQL_Mock_Test_2025.docx Q2 (1 pt)
entries.question: How many distinct countries/regions has each employee shipped orders to?
entries.answer:
SELECT e.ID, e.`Last Name`, e.`First Name`,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.`Ship Country/Region`) AS n_countries
FROM employees AS e
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.`Employee ID` = e.ID
GROUP BY e.ID, e.`Last Name`, e.`First Name`;
entries.explanation: COUNT(DISTINCT col) per employee. LEFT JOIN keeps employees without orders (count 0). The shipping country is the order column `Ship Country/Region`, not the employee's own country. Add `AND o.`Shipped Date` IS NOT NULL` in the ON clause if only already-shipped orders count. In this dump every order ships to 'USA', so each count is 0 or 1.
mistakes: COUNT(o.`Ship Country/Region`) without DISTINCT counts orders.
INNER JOIN drops employees with no orders.
Using employees.`Country/Region` instead of orders.`Ship Country/Region`.
WHERE `Shipped Date` IS NOT NULL after a LEFT JOIN removes zero-count employees.

entries.sourceRef: SQL_Mock_Test_2025.docx Q3 (1 pt)
entries.question: Retrieve the average discount applied to orders shipped to USA.
entries.answer:
SELECT AVG(od.Discount) AS avg_discount
FROM `order details` AS od
JOIN orders AS o ON o.`Order ID` = od.`Order ID`
WHERE o.`Ship Country/Region` = 'USA';
entries.explanation: Discount lives in `order details`; the destination lives in `orders`. Join on `Order ID`, filter on the order's ship country. Add `AND o.`Shipped Date` IS NOT NULL` if 'shipped' means already shipped. All discounts are 0 in this dump, so the result is 0.
mistakes: Filtering customers.`Country/Region` instead of orders.`Ship Country/Region`.
Averaging per order first and then averaging again (changes the weighting).
Querying only `orders` (it has no Discount column).

entries.sourceRef: SQL_Mock_Test_2025.docx Q4 (1 pt)
entries.question: Return the State/Province with only one customer and the customer details (First Name, Last Name) in those states.
entries.answer:
SELECT `State/Province`, `First Name`, `Last Name`
FROM customers
WHERE `State/Province` IN (
    SELECT `State/Province` FROM customers
    GROUP BY `State/Province`
    HAVING COUNT(*) = 1);
entries.explanation: Find states with exactly one customer (GROUP BY + HAVING COUNT(*) = 1), then return that customer's details. A plain GROUP BY cannot return the name columns, so use the grouped query as a subquery (or a window COUNT).
mistakes: Selecting First/Last Name next to GROUP BY `State/Province` (non-aggregated columns).
`HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` or `>= 1` instead of `= 1`.
Putting COUNT(*) = 1 in WHERE.

entries.sourceRef: SQL_Mock_Test_2025.docx Q5 (1 pt)
entries.question:
You need to retrieve unique product categories in the Northwind Database. Which query is better? Explain why.
Query 1 (Using DISTINCT):
SELECT DISTINCT Category FROM Products;
Query 2 (Using GROUP BY):
SELECT Category FROM Products GROUP BY Category;.
entries.answer: Both return the same set of unique categories. DISTINCT is better here: it states the intent (remove duplicates), is shorter, and MySQL 8 normally runs both with the same plan (a temporary table or index scan). GROUP BY is only needed when aggregates are computed per group (COUNT, SUM ...) or HAVING is used. Also: GROUP BY is not an implicit sort in MySQL 8.
examples: SELECT DISTINCT Category FROM products;
SELECT Category FROM products GROUP BY Category;
entries.explanation: Query 1 (DISTINCT) is preferred for pure de-duplication; GROUP BY is for per-group aggregation.
mistakes: Claiming GROUP BY is always faster or always slower.
Assuming GROUP BY sorts the output in MySQL 8.

verification.note: Authored explanation; example queries executed OK

entries.sourceRef: SQL_Mock_Test_2025.docx Q6 (2 pt)
entries.question: Retrieve (all columns) 3 orders which have the 6th, 7th, and 8th highest shipping fee.
entries.answer:
SELECT *
FROM orders
ORDER BY `Shipping Fee` DESC, `Order ID`
LIMIT 3 OFFSET 5;
entries.alternative:
SELECT `Order ID`, `Employee ID`, `Customer ID`, `Order Date`, `Shipped Date`, `Shipper ID`, `Ship Name`, `Ship Address`, `Ship City`, `Ship State/Province`, `Ship ZIP/Postal Code`, `Ship Country/Region`, `Shipping Fee`, `Taxes`, `Payment Type`, `Paid Date`, `Notes`, `Tax Rate`, `Tax Status`, `Status ID`
FROM (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY `Shipping Fee` DESC, `Order ID`) AS rn FROM orders) t
WHERE rn BETWEEN 6 AND 8
ORDER BY rn;
entries.explanation: '3 orders' => row positions 6-8: LIMIT 3 OFFSET 5 (OFFSET is 0-based). Many orders share the same fee, so add a tie-breaker (`Order ID`) for a deterministic result. If '6th highest' means 6th distinct fee value, use DENSE_RANK instead (see the variation).
mistakes: OFFSET 6 (skips 6 rows, so starts at the 7th).
LIMIT 6, 8 (second number is a count, not an end position).
No tie-breaker in ORDER BY.
Confusing row position with distinct value rank.

entries.sourceRef: SQL_Mock_Test_2025.docx Q7 (1 pt)
entries.question: Retrieves the employee who processed the highest number of orders across all months combined in 2006.
entries.answer:
SELECT `Employee ID`, COUNT(*) AS n_orders
FROM orders
WHERE `Order Date` >= '2006-01-01' AND `Order Date` < '2007-01-01'
GROUP BY `Employee ID`
HAVING COUNT(*) = (
    SELECT MAX(c) FROM (
        SELECT COUNT(*) AS c FROM orders
        WHERE `Order Date` >= '2006-01-01' AND `Order Date` < '2007-01-01'
        GROUP BY `Employee ID`) AS t);
entries.alternative:
SELECT `Employee ID`, n_orders
FROM (SELECT `Employee ID`, COUNT(*) AS n_orders, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) AS rk
      FROM orders
      WHERE YEAR(`Order Date`) = 2006
      GROUP BY `Employee ID`) t
WHERE rk = 1;
entries.explanation: 'Across all months combined' = one count per employee for the whole of 2006 (not per month). Compare with the maximum of those counts so ties are all returned. `ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 1` is simpler but drops tied employees. Join `employees` to show names.
mistakes: Grouping by month as well (counts per month, not combined).
LIMIT 1 hides ties.
BETWEEN '2006-01-01' AND '2006-12-31' misses times on Dec 31.
WHERE COUNT(*) = MAX(...) (aggregate in WHERE).

entries.sourceRef: SQL_Mock_Test_2025.docx Q8 (1 pt)
entries.question: Which employees have never processed an order for a customer from the same city they are based in?
entries.answer:
SELECT e.ID, e.`Last Name`, e.`First Name`
FROM employees AS e
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN customers AS c ON c.ID = o.`Customer ID`
    WHERE o.`Employee ID` = e.ID
      AND c.City = e.City);
entries.alternative:
SELECT e.ID, e.`Last Name`, e.`First Name`
FROM employees AS e
LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT o.`Employee ID` AS eid, c.City AS city
           FROM orders AS o JOIN customers AS c ON c.ID = o.`Customer ID`) x
       ON x.eid = e.ID AND x.city = e.City
WHERE x.eid IS NULL;
entries.explanation: 'Never' = anti-join. Inside NOT EXISTS find orders by this employee whose customer is in the employee's own city; keep employees for whom none exist. Includes employees with no orders at all.
mistakes: INNER JOIN with `c.City <> e.City` returns employees who handled SOME other-city order, not those who NEVER handled a same-city one.
NOT IN over a nullable subquery.
Comparing cities with orders.`Ship City` instead of customers.City.

entries.sourceRef: SQL_Mock_Test_2025.docx Q9 (1 pt)
entries.answer: Reasons it is inefficient: (1) SELECT * reads every column although only 3 are needed (more I/O and network, prevents covering-index use); (2) `Order Date` has no index, so MySQL does a full table scan and filters row by row; (3) the range is open-ended and may return a large part of the table. Fix: select only `Order ID`, `Customer ID`, `Order Date`; create an index on `Order Date` (ideally covering: `Order Date`, `Customer ID`); add an upper bound if only a period is needed; do not wrap the column in a function.
examples: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_date_cust ON orders (`Order Date`, `Customer ID`);
entries.explanation: Select only needed columns, index the filter column, keep the predicate sargable, check with EXPLAIN.
mistakes: Only mentioning the index and forgetting SELECT *.
Wrapping `Order Date` in DATE()/YEAR() (disables the index).
Using the `order_id, customer_id, order_date` names from the question: real columns are `Order ID`, `Customer ID`, `Order Date`.

verification.note: Authored explanation; example queries executed OK

entries.sourceRef: SQL_Mock_Test_2025.docx Q10 (1 pt)
entries.question:
You need to retrieve the top 10 most expensive products in the Northwind Database. Which query is better? Explain why.
Query 1:
SELECT * FROM Products
ORDER BY `List Price` DESC
LIMIT 10;
Query 2:
SELECT * FROM Products
WHERE `List Price` >= (SELECT MIN(`List Price`) FROM
(SELECT `List Price` FROM Products ORDER BY `List Price` DESC LIMIT 10) t);
entries.answer: Query 1 is better: it sorts once and stops after 10 rows (ORDER BY ... LIMIT can use a top-N heap/index), it is short and returns exactly 10 rows. Query 2 reads the table twice (derived table + outer scan), is longer and, because of `>=`, returns MORE than 10 rows when prices tie at the 10th place. Use Query 2's idea (or DENSE_RANK/RANK) only if ties must be included. Add a tie-breaker to Query 1 for deterministic output.
examples: SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY `List Price` DESC, ID LIMIT 10;
entries.explanation: LIMIT is simpler and cheaper; the threshold query changes semantics when ties exist.
mistakes: Saying the queries are always equivalent (they differ on ties).
No tie-breaker in ORDER BY.

verification.note: Authored explanation; example queries executed OK

entries.sourceRef: SQL_Mock_Test_2025.docx Q11 (1 pt)
entries.question: Return all the Product Code, Product Name, Category, List Price, Standard Cost and Profit Margin (which can be computed as (List Price - Standard Cost)/ Standard Cost) of products, with Profit Margin larger or equal to 50%. The table products should contain all the needed information for this query.
entries.answer:
SELECT `Product Code`, `Product Name`, Category, `List Price`, `Standard Cost`,
       (`List Price` - `Standard Cost`) / `Standard Cost` AS `Profit Margin`
FROM products
WHERE (`List Price` - `Standard Cost`) / `Standard Cost` >= 0.5;
entries.explanation: A column alias cannot be used in WHERE (evaluated before SELECT), so repeat the expression or wrap it in a derived table. 50% = 0.5. Only `products` is needed.
mistakes: `WHERE `Profit Margin` >= 0.5` (unknown column).
Writing 50 instead of 0.5.
`>` instead of `>=`.
Integer division concerns do not apply: the columns are DECIMAL.

entries.sourceRef: SQL_Mock_Test_2025.docx Q12 (2 pt)
entries.question: Find customers who placed orders for products from more than 3 different categories (Hint: You might need to take a look at several tables)
entries.answer:
SELECT c.ID, c.`Company`, COUNT(DISTINCT p.Category) AS n_categories
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o ON o.`Customer ID` = c.ID
JOIN `order details` AS od ON od.`Order ID` = o.`Order ID`
JOIN products AS p ON p.ID = od.`Product ID`
GROUP BY c.ID, c.`Company`
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT p.Category) > 3;
entries.alternative:
SELECT c.ID, c.`Company`, t.n AS n_categories
FROM customers AS c
JOIN (SELECT o.`Customer ID` AS cid, COUNT(DISTINCT p.Category) AS n
      FROM orders AS o
      JOIN `order details` AS od ON od.`Order ID` = o.`Order ID`
      JOIN products AS p ON p.ID = od.`Product ID`
      GROUP BY o.`Customer ID`) t ON t.cid = c.ID
WHERE t.n > 3;
entries.explanation: Chain customers -> orders -> `order details` -> products (category is a column of products). COUNT(DISTINCT Category) per customer, filter in HAVING. 'More than 3' is `> 3`; 'at least 3' would be `>= 3`.
mistakes: COUNT(p.Category) without DISTINCT counts order lines.
`>= 3` for 'more than 3'.
Condition in WHERE instead of HAVING.
Skipping the `orders` table (customers do not link to `order details` directly).

entries.sourceRef: SQL_Mock_Test_2025.docx Q13 (2 pt)
entries.question: Given the Total Value can be computed as SUM of Unit Price * Quantity, retrieve Order ID, Total Value and Shipping Fee of each order, then only display those with Shipping Fee > 15% of Total Value. You should also return a column showing the ratio between Shipping Fee and Total Value (i.e., Shipping Fee/ Total Value), this column should be rounded to 4 decimal places.
entries.answer:
SELECT o.`Order ID`, t.total_value AS `Total Value`, o.`Shipping Fee`,
       ROUND(o.`Shipping Fee` / t.total_value, 4) AS ratio
FROM orders AS o
JOIN (SELECT `Order ID`, SUM(`Unit Price` * Quantity) AS total_value
      FROM `order details`
      GROUP BY `Order ID`) AS t ON t.`Order ID` = o.`Order ID`
WHERE o.`Shipping Fee` > 0.15 * t.total_value;
entries.alternative:
SELECT o.`Order ID`, SUM(od.`Unit Price` * od.Quantity) AS `Total Value`, o.`Shipping Fee`,
       ROUND(o.`Shipping Fee` / SUM(od.`Unit Price` * od.Quantity), 4) AS ratio
FROM orders AS o
JOIN `order details` AS od ON od.`Order ID` = o.`Order ID`
GROUP BY o.`Order ID`, o.`Shipping Fee`
HAVING o.`Shipping Fee` > 0.15 * SUM(od.`Unit Price` * od.Quantity);
entries.explanation: Total value per order = SUM(`Unit Price` * Quantity) over `order details`. Aggregate first (derived table, or GROUP BY with HAVING), then compare the order's own fee. 'Shipping fee > 15% of total' is strict `>`. ROUND(x, 4) for four decimals. The question's definition ignores Discount.
mistakes: Comparing fee to a per-line value instead of the order total.
Aggregate in WHERE.
Joining and summing without grouping (fee repeated per line).
`>=` instead of `>`.
Forgetting ROUND(..., 4).

entries.sourceRef: SQL_Mock_Test_2025.docx Q14 (2 pt)
entries.question:
From the inventory transactions table, write an SQL query to compute the total quantity of each product (Product ID) for each month, using the Transaction Created Date column as the date of the transaction. The result should also include Product name, and you should only include inventory transactions with status = ‘Sold’. There should be 4 columns in your results:
Month: The month in which the transactions occurred, in the format 'YYYY-MM'.
Product ID: The ID of the product.
Product Name: The name of the product.
Total Quantity: The total quantity of the inventory sold in that month.
entries.answer:
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(it.`Transaction Created Date`, '%Y-%m') AS `Month`,
       it.`Product ID`,
       p.`Product Name`,
       SUM(it.Quantity) AS `Total Quantity`
FROM `inventory transactions` AS it
JOIN `inventory transaction types` AS tt ON tt.ID = it.`Transaction Type`
JOIN products AS p ON p.ID = it.`Product ID`
WHERE tt.`Type Name` = 'Sold'
GROUP BY `Month`, it.`Product ID`, p.`Product Name`;
entries.alternative:
SELECT CONCAT(YEAR(it.`Transaction Created Date`), '-', LPAD(MONTH(it.`Transaction Created Date`), 2, '0')) AS `Month`,
       it.`Product ID`, p.`Product Name`, SUM(it.Quantity) AS `Total Quantity`
FROM `inventory transactions` AS it
JOIN products AS p ON p.ID = it.`Product ID`
WHERE it.`Transaction Type` = 2
GROUP BY 1, it.`Product ID`, p.`Product Name`;
entries.explanation: `inventory transactions` has NO 'Status' column: the status is `Transaction Type`, an ID into `inventory transaction types` (`Type Name` = 'Sold', ID 2). Month key: DATE_FORMAT(..., '%Y-%m'). Product name comes from `products`.
mistakes: `WHERE Status = 'Sold'` (column does not exist).
`Transaction Type = 'Sold'` (it holds a number).
Using %i (minutes) instead of %m (month).
Grouping only by month, losing the product.
Month number without year.

entries.sourceRef: SQL_Mock_Test_2025.docx Q15 (2 pt)
entries.question: Find products that have been ordered together most frequently (Hint: Using seft join).
entries.answer:
SELECT a.`Product ID` AS product_1, b.`Product ID` AS product_2, COUNT(DISTINCT a.`Order ID`) AS times_together
FROM `order details` AS a
JOIN `order details` AS b ON a.`Order ID` = b.`Order ID` AND a.`Product ID` < b.`Product ID`
GROUP BY a.`Product ID`, b.`Product ID`
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT a.`Order ID`) = (
    SELECT MAX(n) FROM (
        SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT x.`Order ID`) AS n
        FROM `order details` AS x
        JOIN `order details` AS y ON x.`Order ID` = y.`Order ID` AND x.`Product ID` < y.`Product ID`
        GROUP BY x.`Product ID`, y.`Product ID`) AS t);
entries.alternative:
SELECT product_1, product_2, times_together
FROM (SELECT a.`Product ID` AS product_1, b.`Product ID` AS product_2, COUNT(DISTINCT a.`Order ID`) AS times_together,
             RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(DISTINCT a.`Order ID`) DESC) AS rk
      FROM `order details` AS a
      JOIN `order details` AS b ON a.`Order ID` = b.`Order ID` AND a.`Product ID` < b.`Product ID`
      GROUP BY a.`Product ID`, b.`Product ID`) t
WHERE rk = 1;
entries.explanation: Self join `order details` on the same Order ID. `a.`Product ID` < b.`Product ID`` drops self-pairs and the mirrored duplicate (1,43)/(43,1). Count orders per pair; compare with the maximum so tied top pairs are all returned (several pairs tie at 2 here).
mistakes: `<>` returns every pair twice.
Missing the Order ID join condition (cartesian product).
COUNT(*) without DISTINCT if a product can repeat in an order.
LIMIT 1 hides tied pairs.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q1
entries.question: Summarise the product catalogue in a single row: the number of products, the number of distinct categories, and the minimum, maximum and average List Price (average rounded to 2 decimals).
entries.answer:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS n_products,
       COUNT(DISTINCT Category) AS n_categories,
       MIN(`List Price`) AS min_price,
       MAX(`List Price`) AS max_price,
       ROUND(AVG(`List Price`), 2) AS avg_price
FROM products;
entries.alternative:
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products), (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT Category FROM products GROUP BY Category) t),
       (SELECT MIN(`List Price`) FROM products), (SELECT MAX(`List Price`) FROM products), (SELECT ROUND(SUM(`List Price`) / COUNT(`List Price`), 2) FROM products);
entries.explanation: No GROUP BY: all aggregates collapse the whole table into one row. COUNT(DISTINCT Category) counts different categories.
mistakes: COUNT(Category) without DISTINCT counts products.
Forgetting ROUND(..., 2) on the average.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q2
entries.question: In the orders table, compare COUNT(*) with COUNT(`Shipped Date`), COUNT(`Shipper ID`) and COUNT(`Payment Type`). Also return the number of orders that have not been shipped yet, computed only from these counts (no WHERE clause). In one sentence, explain why the four counts differ.
entries.answer:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_orders,
       COUNT(`Shipped Date`) AS with_shipped_date,
       COUNT(`Shipper ID`) AS with_shipper,
       COUNT(`Payment Type`) AS with_payment_type,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(`Shipped Date`) AS not_shipped_yet
FROM orders;
entries.alternative: SELECT SUM(1), SUM(`Shipped Date` IS NOT NULL), SUM(`Shipper ID` IS NOT NULL), SUM(`Payment Type` IS NOT NULL), SUM(`Shipped Date` IS NULL) FROM orders;
entries.explanation: One sentence: COUNT(*) counts every row, while COUNT(column) counts only rows where that column is NOT NULL, and the four columns contain different numbers of NULLs. Not-shipped = COUNT(*) - COUNT(`Shipped Date`) (no WHERE needed).
mistakes: Using COUNT(*) for every column.
WHERE `Shipped Date` IS NULL when the question forbids WHERE.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q3
entries.question: Using `order details`, compute the line value of each row as Quantity * `Unit Price` * (1 - Discount). Return in one row: the total sales value, the average line value and the largest single line value (all rounded to 2 decimals).
entries.answer:
SELECT ROUND(SUM(Quantity * `Unit Price` * (1 - Discount)), 2) AS total_sales,
       ROUND(AVG(Quantity * `Unit Price` * (1 - Discount)), 2) AS avg_line_value,
       ROUND(MAX(Quantity * `Unit Price` * (1 - Discount)), 2) AS max_line_value
FROM `order details`;
entries.alternative:
SELECT ROUND(SUM(v), 2), ROUND(AVG(v), 2), ROUND(MAX(v), 2)
FROM (SELECT Quantity * `Unit Price` * (1 - Discount) AS v FROM `order details`) t;
entries.explanation: Compute the line value inside the aggregate (or in a derived table). Discount is a fraction (0.1 = 10%).
mistakes: Discount instead of (1 - Discount).
Averaging the order totals instead of the lines.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q4
entries.question: For each product category, show the number of products and the average List Price (2 decimals). Sort by number of products descending, then by category name.
entries.answer:
SELECT Category, COUNT(*) AS n_products, ROUND(AVG(`List Price`), 2) AS avg_price
FROM products
GROUP BY Category
ORDER BY n_products DESC, Category;
entries.explanation: GROUP BY category with two aggregates; ORDER BY can use the alias n_products.
mistakes: ORDER BY n_products without DESC.
Sorting by category first.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q5
entries.question: For each product, compute the total quantity sold in `order details`. Show only products whose total quantity is at least 100, sorted from highest to lowest. Return the Product ID and the total quantity.
entries.answer:
SELECT `Product ID`, SUM(Quantity) AS total_quantity
FROM `order details`
GROUP BY `Product ID`
HAVING SUM(Quantity) >= 100
ORDER BY total_quantity DESC, `Product ID`;
entries.alternative:
SELECT `Product ID`, total_quantity
FROM (SELECT `Product ID`, SUM(Quantity) AS total_quantity FROM `order details` GROUP BY `Product ID`) t
WHERE total_quantity >= 100
ORDER BY total_quantity DESC, `Product ID`;
entries.explanation: The condition is on an aggregate, so it goes in HAVING (or WHERE of a derived table). 'At least 100' is >= 100.
mistakes: WHERE SUM(Quantity) >= 100 (aggregate in WHERE).
> 100 instead of >= 100.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q6
entries.question: Considering only orders whose `Status ID` is 3 (Closed), find the customers who have at least 3 such orders. For each, show the Customer ID, the number of closed orders, the total shipping fee (2 decimals), and the dates of their first and last closed order. Explain which condition belongs in WHERE and which belongs in HAVING.
entries.answer:
SELECT `Customer ID`,
       COUNT(*) AS n_closed,
       ROUND(SUM(`Shipping Fee`), 2) AS total_shipping_fee,
       MIN(`Order Date`) AS first_closed_order,
       MAX(`Order Date`) AS last_closed_order
FROM orders
WHERE `Status ID` = 3
GROUP BY `Customer ID`
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
entries.alternative:
SELECT cid, n, ROUND(f, 2), d1, d2
FROM (SELECT `Customer ID` AS cid, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(`Shipping Fee`) AS f, MIN(`Order Date`) AS d1, MAX(`Order Date`) AS d2
      FROM orders WHERE `Status ID` = 3 GROUP BY `Customer ID`) t
WHERE n >= 3;
entries.explanation: WHERE `Status ID` = 3 filters rows BEFORE grouping (only closed orders are counted). HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 filters the groups AFTER aggregation. Moving Status ID to HAVING is invalid (not aggregated); moving the count to WHERE is impossible.
mistakes: Counting all orders and then filtering status.
COUNT(*) >= 3 in WHERE.
> 3 instead of >= 3.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q7
entries.question: List every order placed in March 2006 with the order ID, order date, customer company, and the first and last name of the employee who took it. Sort by order date, then order ID.
entries.answer:
SELECT o.`Order ID`, o.`Order Date`, c.Company, e.`First Name`, e.`Last Name`
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON c.ID = o.`Customer ID`
JOIN employees AS e ON e.ID = o.`Employee ID`
WHERE o.`Order Date` >= '2006-03-01' AND o.`Order Date` < '2006-04-01'
ORDER BY o.`Order Date`, o.`Order ID`;
entries.alternative:
SELECT o.`Order ID`, o.`Order Date`, c.Company, e.`First Name`, e.`Last Name`
FROM orders o, customers c, employees e
WHERE c.ID = o.`Customer ID` AND e.ID = o.`Employee ID` AND YEAR(o.`Order Date`) = 2006 AND MONTH(o.`Order Date`) = 3
ORDER BY o.`Order Date`, o.`Order ID`;
entries.explanation: Join orders to customers and employees through the key columns; a half-open date range avoids the BETWEEN datetime pitfall.
mistakes: BETWEEN '2006-03-01' AND '2006-03-31' misses March 31 after 00:00:00.
Joining customers/employees on the wrong column.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q8
entries.question: List every customer together with the number of orders they have placed, including customers who have never placed an order (they must show 0). Show the customers with no orders first, then sort by company. Explain why COUNT(*) would give the wrong answer here.
entries.answer:
SELECT c.ID, c.Company, COUNT(o.`Order ID`) AS n_orders
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.`Customer ID` = c.ID
GROUP BY c.ID, c.Company
ORDER BY (COUNT(o.`Order ID`) > 0), c.Company;
entries.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps customers without orders; COUNT(o.`Order ID`) counts only matched rows, so they get 0. COUNT(*) would count the single NULL-extended row and return 1 for customers with no orders. (count > 0) is 0 for the zero-order customers, so they sort first.
mistakes: COUNT(*) gives 1 for customers without orders.
INNER JOIN drops customers without orders.
WHERE on orders columns turns the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q9
entries.question: Count orders per shipper so that the result includes (a) shippers with no orders and (b) orders that have no shipper assigned. Emulate a FULL OUTER JOIN between shippers and orders by combining a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN with UNION. Show the shipper ID, the shipper company and the number of orders.
entries.answer:
SELECT s.ID AS shipper_id, s.Company, COUNT(o.`Order ID`) AS n_orders
FROM shippers AS s
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.`Shipper ID` = s.ID
GROUP BY s.ID, s.Company
UNION
SELECT s.ID, s.Company, COUNT(o.`Order ID`)
FROM shippers AS s
RIGHT JOIN orders AS o ON o.`Shipper ID` = s.ID
GROUP BY s.ID, s.Company;
entries.alternative:
SELECT s.ID, s.Company, COUNT(o.`Order ID`)
FROM shippers AS s LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.`Shipper ID` = s.ID
GROUP BY s.ID, s.Company
UNION ALL
SELECT NULL, NULL, COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE `Shipper ID` IS NULL;
entries.explanation: MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN: LEFT JOIN (all shippers) UNION RIGHT JOIN (all orders). UNION (not UNION ALL) removes the shipper rows that both halves return. The RIGHT JOIN half produces the group with shipper NULL for orders without a shipper (5 here).
mistakes: UNION ALL duplicates the matched shipper rows.
Grouping before the UNION on only one half.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q10
entries.question: Build a grid of every shipper combined with every payment type that appears in orders, and show how many orders used each combination, including combinations with 0 orders. Use a CROSS JOIN to build the grid, then a LEFT JOIN to count orders.
entries.answer:
SELECT s.ID AS shipper_id, s.Company, pt.`Payment Type`, COUNT(o.`Order ID`) AS n_orders
FROM shippers AS s
CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT `Payment Type` FROM orders WHERE `Payment Type` IS NOT NULL) AS pt
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.`Shipper ID` = s.ID AND o.`Payment Type` = pt.`Payment Type`
GROUP BY s.ID, s.Company, pt.`Payment Type`;
entries.explanation: CROSS JOIN builds every shipper x payment-type combination; LEFT JOIN with both conditions in ON counts matching orders (0 stays 0). Conditions on orders must be in ON, not WHERE.
mistakes: Putting o.`Payment Type` = ... in WHERE (drops zero combinations).
COUNT(*) instead of COUNT(o.`Order ID`).

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q11
entries.question: Find every pair of different customers located in the same city. Show the city and both company names, list each pair only once (no reversed duplicates), and sort by city.
entries.answer:
SELECT a.City, a.Company AS company_1, b.Company AS company_2
FROM customers AS a
JOIN customers AS b ON a.City = b.City AND a.ID < b.ID
ORDER BY a.City, a.ID, b.ID;
entries.alternative: SELECT a.City, a.Company, b.Company FROM customers a, customers b WHERE a.City = b.City AND a.ID < b.ID ORDER BY a.City, a.ID, b.ID;
entries.explanation: a.ID < b.ID removes self-pairs and reversed duplicates (a<>b would list every pair twice).
mistakes: <> returns each pair twice.
Missing the city condition.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q12
entries.question: Product Code is supposed to identify a product uniquely, but the data contains duplicates. Use a self join on products to list every pair of different products that share the same Product Code. Show the code and both product IDs and names.
entries.alternative: SELECT a.`Product Code`, a.ID, a.`Product Name`, b.ID, b.`Product Name` FROM products a, products b WHERE a.`Product Code` = b.`Product Code` AND a.ID <> b.ID AND a.ID < b.ID;
entries.explanation: Self join on the supposedly unique column; a.ID < b.ID keeps each duplicate pair once.
mistakes: a.ID <> b.ID lists each pair twice.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q13
entries.question: For every purchase order, show the purchase order ID, the supplier company, the status text from `purchase order status`, the last name of the employee who created it and the last name of the employee who approved it. All 28 purchase orders must appear, even when the creator or approver is unknown. Sort by purchase order ID.
entries.answer:
SELECT po.`Purchase Order ID`, s.Company AS supplier, pos.Status AS status_text,
       cr.`Last Name` AS created_by, ap.`Last Name` AS approved_by
FROM `purchase orders` AS po
LEFT JOIN suppliers AS s ON s.ID = po.`Supplier ID`
LEFT JOIN `purchase order status` AS pos ON pos.`Status ID` = po.`Status ID`
LEFT JOIN employees AS cr ON cr.ID = po.`Created By`
LEFT JOIN employees AS ap ON ap.ID = po.`Approved By`
ORDER BY po.`Purchase Order ID`;
entries.alternative:
SELECT po.`Purchase Order ID`,
       (SELECT s.Company FROM suppliers s WHERE s.ID = po.`Supplier ID`),
       (SELECT x.Status FROM `purchase order status` x WHERE x.`Status ID` = po.`Status ID`),
       (SELECT e.`Last Name` FROM employees e WHERE e.ID = po.`Created By`),
       (SELECT e.`Last Name` FROM employees e WHERE e.ID = po.`Approved By`)
FROM `purchase orders` po ORDER BY po.`Purchase Order ID`;
entries.explanation: Join `employees` twice with different aliases (creator, approver). LEFT JOINs keep all 28 purchase orders even when Created By / Approved By is NULL. The status text column is `purchase order status`.`Status`.
mistakes: INNER JOIN drops purchase orders with NULL creator/approver.
Using the same alias for both employee joins.
Looking for a `Status Name` column (it is `Status` here).

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q14
entries.question: Using a scalar subquery, list the products whose List Price is above the average List Price of all products. Show the product name, the list price and the difference from the average (2 decimals), most expensive first.
entries.answer:
SELECT `Product Name`, `List Price`,
       ROUND(`List Price` - (SELECT AVG(`List Price`) FROM products), 2) AS diff_from_avg
FROM products
WHERE `List Price` > (SELECT AVG(`List Price`) FROM products)
ORDER BY `List Price` DESC, `Product Name`;
entries.alternative:
SELECT `Product Name`, `List Price`, ROUND(`List Price` - a, 2)
FROM (SELECT *, AVG(`List Price`) OVER () AS a FROM products) t
WHERE `List Price` > a
ORDER BY `List Price` DESC, `Product Name`;
entries.explanation: A scalar subquery returns one value (the overall average) and can be used in WHERE and in SELECT.
mistakes: AVG(...) directly in WHERE.
Subquery that returns more than one row.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q15
entries.question: Using a correlated subquery, find the most expensive product in each category (if several products tie, show all of them). Show the category, product name and list price, sorted by category.
entries.answer:
SELECT p.Category, p.`Product Name`, p.`List Price`
FROM products AS p
WHERE p.`List Price` = (SELECT MAX(q.`List Price`) FROM products AS q WHERE q.Category = p.Category)
ORDER BY p.Category, p.`Product Name`;
entries.alternative:
SELECT Category, `Product Name`, `List Price`
FROM (SELECT *, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY Category ORDER BY `List Price` DESC) AS rk FROM products) t
WHERE rk = 1
ORDER BY Category, `Product Name`;
entries.explanation: Compare each product with the maximum of ITS OWN category (correlation q.Category = p.Category). Equality with MAX keeps all tied products, unlike LIMIT 1.
mistakes: Forgetting the correlation (global max).
LIMIT 1 or GROUP BY with non-aggregated columns.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q16
entries.question: Find the customers who have ordered at least one product from the 'Beverages' category. Write the query twice, once with IN and once with EXISTS, and check that both return the same rows. Show the customer ID and company.
entries.answer:
SELECT c.ID, c.Company
FROM customers AS c
WHERE c.ID IN (
    SELECT o.`Customer ID`
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN `order details` AS od ON od.`Order ID` = o.`Order ID`
    JOIN products AS p ON p.ID = od.`Product ID`
    WHERE p.Category = 'Beverages');
entries.alternative:
SELECT c.ID, c.Company
FROM customers AS c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN `order details` AS od ON od.`Order ID` = o.`Order ID`
    JOIN products AS p ON p.ID = od.`Product ID`
    WHERE o.`Customer ID` = c.ID AND p.Category = 'Beverages');
entries.explanation: Main = IN version, alternative = EXISTS version; the build compares both result sets (identical). IN tests membership of the set of customer IDs, EXISTS probes per customer with a correlation.
mistakes: Forgetting the correlation in EXISTS.
Joining directly and returning duplicate customers (needs DISTINCT).

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q17
entries.question: Find the employees who never created a purchase order. First try WHERE ID NOT IN (SELECT `Created By` FROM `purchase orders`) and observe the result. Then write a version with NOT EXISTS that returns the correct answer. Explain why the NOT IN version fails.
entries.answer:
SELECT e.ID, e.`Last Name`
FROM employees AS e
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM `purchase orders` AS po WHERE po.`Created By` = e.ID);

-- also asked / related:
SELECT ID FROM employees WHERE ID NOT IN (SELECT `Created By` FROM `purchase orders`);  -- returns nothing: the NULL trap
entries.alternative:
SELECT e.ID, e.`Last Name`
FROM employees AS e
LEFT JOIN `purchase orders` AS po ON po.`Created By` = e.ID
WHERE po.`Created By` IS NULL;
entries.explanation: `purchase orders`.`Created By` contains NULLs. With NOT IN, the list contains NULL, so `ID NOT IN (..., NULL)` is UNKNOWN for every row and the query returns NO rows. NOT EXISTS ignores NULLs and returns the correct employee(s).
mistakes: Trusting an empty NOT IN result.
Inner join with <>.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q18
entries.question: Using a row subquery, find all orders placed by the same customer AND taken by the same employee as order 30 (exclude order 30 itself). Show the order ID, customer ID, employee ID and order date.
entries.answer:
SELECT `Order ID`, `Customer ID`, `Employee ID`, `Order Date`
FROM orders
WHERE (`Customer ID`, `Employee ID`) = (SELECT `Customer ID`, `Employee ID` FROM orders WHERE `Order ID` = 30)
  AND `Order ID` <> 30;
entries.explanation: Row constructor (a, b) = (subquery returning one row with two columns) compares both columns at once; exclude order 30 itself.
mistakes: Comparing columns separately with two subqueries.
Forgetting to exclude order 30.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q19
entries.question: Build one contact directory of all customers, employees and suppliers with the columns contact_type ('Customer', 'Employee' or 'Supplier'), company, first_name, last_name and city. Sort by contact_type, then last_name. Then write a second query that returns how many rows a UNION ALL of the customer cities and employee cities produces, and how many a UNION produces. Explain the difference.
entries.answer:
SELECT 'Customer' AS contact_type, Company, `First Name` AS first_name, `Last Name` AS last_name, City FROM customers
UNION ALL
SELECT 'Employee', Company, `First Name`, `Last Name`, City FROM employees
UNION ALL
SELECT 'Supplier', Company, `First Name`, `Last Name`, City FROM suppliers
ORDER BY contact_type, last_name;

-- also asked / related:
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT City FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT City FROM employees) a) AS union_all_rows,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT City FROM customers UNION SELECT City FROM employees) b) AS union_rows;
entries.alternative:
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT 'Customer' AS contact_type, Company, `First Name` AS first_name, `Last Name` AS last_name, City FROM customers
  UNION
  SELECT 'Employee', Company, `First Name`, `Last Name`, City FROM employees
  UNION
  SELECT 'Supplier', Company, `First Name`, `Last Name`, City FROM suppliers) t
ORDER BY contact_type, last_name;
entries.explanation: UNION ALL stacks the three result sets (same column count/order; the first SELECT names the columns; one ORDER BY at the end). UNION ALL keeps every row, UNION removes duplicate rows, so UNION returns fewer rows when cities repeat (second query).
mistakes: Different column order between the SELECTs.
ORDER BY inside each branch.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q20
entries.question: Find the product IDs that were both sold to customers (`order details`) and bought from suppliers (`purchase order details`). Write it with INTERSECT, then rewrite it with IN and confirm that both return the same rows.
entries.answer:
SELECT DISTINCT `Product ID`
FROM `order details`
WHERE `Product ID` IN (SELECT `Product ID` FROM `purchase order details`);

-- also asked / related:
SELECT `Product ID` FROM `order details` INTERSECT SELECT `Product ID` FROM `purchase order details`;  -- needs MySQL >= 8.0.31
entries.explanation: Main = IN rewrite (works on every MySQL 8.0). INTERSECT is only supported from MySQL 8.0.31, but the dump comes from 8.0.28, so it may fail on the exam server; the alternative is shown for completeness. Both return the same rows (checked at build time).
mistakes: Using INTERSECT on MySQL < 8.0.31 (syntax error).
Forgetting DISTINCT with IN.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q21
entries.question: Find the products that were bought from suppliers but never sold to customers. Write it with EXCEPT, then rewrite it with NOT EXISTS and add the product name to the NOT EXISTS version.
entries.answer:
SELECT DISTINCT p.ID, p.`Product Name`
FROM products AS p
JOIN `purchase order details` AS pod ON pod.`Product ID` = p.ID
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM `order details` AS od WHERE od.`Product ID` = p.ID);

-- also asked / related:
SELECT `Product ID` FROM `purchase order details` EXCEPT SELECT `Product ID` FROM `order details`;  -- needs MySQL >= 8.0.31
entries.alternative:
SELECT ID, `Product Name` FROM products
WHERE ID IN (SELECT `Product ID` FROM `purchase order details` EXCEPT SELECT `Product ID` FROM `order details`);
entries.explanation: Main = NOT EXISTS with the product name (works on 8.0.28). EXCEPT exists only from MySQL 8.0.31; the plain EXCEPT form is shown in the extra statement.
mistakes: EXCEPT on MySQL < 8.0.31.
NOT IN over a nullable column.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q22
entries.question: Produce an employee directory with: the full name in the form 'LASTNAME, First' (last name in upper case), the initials (e.g. 'NF' for Nancy Freehafer), the e-mail address in lower case, the e-mail domain (the part after '@'), and the length of the full name. Sort by last name.
entries.answer:
SELECT CONCAT(UPPER(`Last Name`), ', ', `First Name`) AS full_name,
       CONCAT(LEFT(`First Name`, 1), LEFT(`Last Name`, 1)) AS initials,
       LOWER(`E-mail Address`) AS email,
       SUBSTRING_INDEX(LOWER(`E-mail Address`), '@', -1) AS email_domain,
       CHAR_LENGTH(CONCAT(UPPER(`Last Name`), ', ', `First Name`)) AS name_length
FROM employees
ORDER BY `Last Name`;
entries.alternative:
SELECT CONCAT_WS(', ', UPPER(`Last Name`), `First Name`), CONCAT(SUBSTRING(`First Name`, 1, 1), SUBSTRING(`Last Name`, 1, 1)),
       LOWER(`E-mail Address`), SUBSTRING(LOWER(`E-mail Address`), LOCATE('@', `E-mail Address`) + 1),
       CHAR_LENGTH(UPPER(`Last Name`)) + 2 + CHAR_LENGTH(`First Name`)
FROM employees ORDER BY `Last Name`;
entries.explanation: String functions: CONCAT, UPPER/LOWER, LEFT, SUBSTRING_INDEX(x,'@',-1) = part after '@', CHAR_LENGTH. 'Length of the full name' is taken as the length of the 'LASTNAME, First' string.
mistakes: LENGTH counts bytes, CHAR_LENGTH counts characters.
Initials in the wrong order.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q23
entries.question: Product codes have the form PREFIX-NUMBER (e.g. NWTCFV-17). For each product, show the code, the prefix (the part before '-'), the number (the part after '-'), and a short name obtained by removing the text 'Northwind Traders ' from the product name. Then write a second query that counts products per prefix and shows only prefixes used by at least 3 products.
entries.answer:
SELECT `Product Code`,
       SUBSTRING_INDEX(`Product Code`, '-', 1) AS prefix,
       SUBSTRING_INDEX(`Product Code`, '-', -1) AS number,
       REPLACE(`Product Name`, 'Northwind Traders ', '') AS short_name
FROM products;

-- also asked / related:
SELECT SUBSTRING_INDEX(`Product Code`, '-', 1) AS prefix, COUNT(*) AS n_products
FROM products
GROUP BY SUBSTRING_INDEX(`Product Code`, '-', 1)
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
entries.explanation: SUBSTRING_INDEX(str, '-', 1) = text before the first '-'; with -1 = text after the last '-'. Second query groups by prefix and keeps prefixes used by at least 3 products (see extra).
mistakes: Using SUBSTRING with a fixed length.
Forgetting the trailing space in the prefix text.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q24
entries.question: The `Supplier IDs` column of products stores several supplier IDs in one text value separated by ';' (for example '2;6'). List the products that have more than one supplier, showing the product name, the raw `Supplier IDs` value, the first supplier ID, the last supplier ID and the number of suppliers. Hint: the number of suppliers equals the number of ';' characters plus one, and you can count characters with LENGTH and REPLACE.
entries.answer:
SELECT `Product Name`, `Supplier IDs`,
       SUBSTRING_INDEX(`Supplier IDs`, ';', 1) AS first_supplier,
       SUBSTRING_INDEX(`Supplier IDs`, ';', -1) AS last_supplier,
       LENGTH(`Supplier IDs`) - LENGTH(REPLACE(`Supplier IDs`, ';', '')) + 1 AS n_suppliers
FROM products
WHERE `Supplier IDs` LIKE '%;%';
entries.alternative:
SELECT `Product Name`, `Supplier IDs`, f, l, n
FROM (SELECT *, SUBSTRING_INDEX(`Supplier IDs`, ';', 1) AS f, SUBSTRING_INDEX(`Supplier IDs`, ';', -1) AS l,
             LENGTH(`Supplier IDs`) - LENGTH(REPLACE(`Supplier IDs`, ';', '')) + 1 AS n FROM products) t
WHERE n > 1;
entries.explanation: Number of items = number of ';' + 1; number of ';' = LENGTH(x) - LENGTH(REPLACE(x, ';', '')). Products with more than one supplier contain at least one ';'.
mistakes: Counting the separators and forgetting +1.
Using = on the list instead of LIKE/derived n > 1.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q25
entries.question: Produce a monthly order summary: for each month in which orders were placed, show the month in the format 'YYYY-MM', the month name (e.g. 'January'), the number of orders and the total shipping fee (2 decimals). Sort chronologically.
entries.answer:
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(`Order Date`, '%Y-%m') AS ym,
       MONTHNAME(`Order Date`) AS month_name,
       COUNT(*) AS n_orders,
       ROUND(SUM(`Shipping Fee`), 2) AS total_shipping_fee
FROM orders
GROUP BY ym, month_name
ORDER BY ym;
entries.explanation: Group by the 'YYYY-MM' key (%Y-%m; %i would be minutes). Sorting by that text key is chronological.
mistakes: Grouping by MONTH() only (mixes years).
Sorting by month name (alphabetical).

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q26
entries.question: For shipped orders, the lead time is the number of days between `Order Date` and `Shipped Date`. For each shipper, show the company, the number of shipped orders, the average lead time (1 decimal), the longest lead time and the number of orders shipped on the same day they were placed.
entries.answer:
SELECT s.Company,
       COUNT(*) AS n_shipped,
       ROUND(AVG(DATEDIFF(o.`Shipped Date`, o.`Order Date`)), 1) AS avg_lead_days,
       MAX(DATEDIFF(o.`Shipped Date`, o.`Order Date`)) AS max_lead_days,
       SUM(DATEDIFF(o.`Shipped Date`, o.`Order Date`) = 0) AS shipped_same_day
FROM orders AS o
JOIN shippers AS s ON s.ID = o.`Shipper ID`
WHERE o.`Shipped Date` IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY s.ID, s.Company;
entries.explanation: DATEDIFF(later, earlier) = whole days. WHERE keeps shipped orders only. SUM(condition) counts same-day shipments.
mistakes: DATEDIFF with reversed arguments (negative values).
Including unshipped orders (NULL dates).

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q27
entries.question: The `Due Date` column of invoices is empty. For the invoices, show the invoice ID, the order ID, the invoice date formatted as 'DD/MM/YYYY', the weekday of the invoice date, a computed due date 30 days after the invoice date (DATE_ADD, formatted as 'DD/MM/YYYY'), and how many whole days have passed between that computed due date and today (CURDATE). Show only the 5 earliest invoices. Note that the last column depends on the day you run the query.
entries.answer:
SELECT `Invoice ID`, `Order ID`,
       DATE_FORMAT(`Invoice Date`, '%d/%m/%Y') AS invoice_date,
       DAYNAME(`Invoice Date`) AS weekday,
       DATE_FORMAT(DATE_ADD(`Invoice Date`, INTERVAL 30 DAY), '%d/%m/%Y') AS due_date,
       DATEDIFF(CURDATE(), DATE(DATE_ADD(`Invoice Date`, INTERVAL 30 DAY))) AS days_since_due
FROM invoices
ORDER BY `Invoice Date`, `Invoice ID`
LIMIT 5;
entries.explanation: Due date = invoice date + 30 days. %d/%m/%Y gives DD/MM/YYYY (%M would be the month NAME). The last column depends on the day you run it.
mistakes: %m/%d/%Y order.
DATEDIFF(due, CURDATE()) has the opposite sign.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q28
entries.question: Classify products into price bands using CASE: 'Budget' when List Price is below 5, 'Standard' when it is from 5 up to (but not including) 20, and 'Premium' otherwise. Show each band with the number of products and the average list price (2 decimals), ordered Budget, Standard, Premium.
entries.answer:
SELECT CASE WHEN `List Price` < 5 THEN 'Budget' WHEN `List Price` < 20 THEN 'Standard' ELSE 'Premium' END AS band,
       COUNT(*) AS n_products,
       ROUND(AVG(`List Price`), 2) AS avg_price
FROM products
GROUP BY band
ORDER BY FIELD(band, 'Budget', 'Standard', 'Premium');
entries.alternative:
SELECT band, COUNT(*), ROUND(AVG(`List Price`), 2)
FROM (SELECT *, CASE WHEN `List Price` >= 20 THEN 'Premium' WHEN `List Price` >= 5 THEN 'Standard' ELSE 'Budget' END AS band FROM products) t
GROUP BY band
ORDER BY CASE band WHEN 'Budget' THEN 1 WHEN 'Standard' THEN 2 ELSE 3 END;
entries.explanation: CASE evaluates top-down; 'Standard' = from 5 up to but NOT including 20. FIELD() or CASE gives a custom sort order. Bands with no products do not appear.
mistakes: <= 20 for Standard.
Alphabetical sort of the band names.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q29
entries.question: List the orders that have not been closed (`Status ID` <> 3). For each, show the order ID, the customer company, the shipper company or 'Not assigned' when there is none (IFNULL), the shipped date or the text 'Pending' (IFNULL), the payment state as 'Paid' or 'Unpaid' based on `Paid Date` (IF), and the order status name. Sort by order ID.
entries.answer:
SELECT o.`Order ID`, c.Company AS customer,
       IFNULL(sh.Company, 'Not assigned') AS shipper,
       IFNULL(CAST(o.`Shipped Date` AS CHAR), 'Pending') AS shipped_date,
       IF(o.`Paid Date` IS NULL, 'Unpaid', 'Paid') AS payment_state,
       os.`Status Name`
FROM orders AS o
LEFT JOIN customers AS c ON c.ID = o.`Customer ID`
LEFT JOIN shippers AS sh ON sh.ID = o.`Shipper ID`
LEFT JOIN `orders status` AS os ON os.`Status ID` = o.`Status ID`
WHERE o.`Status ID` <> 3
ORDER BY o.`Order ID`;
entries.alternative:
SELECT o.`Order ID`, c.Company, COALESCE(sh.Company, 'Not assigned'), COALESCE(DATE_FORMAT(o.`Shipped Date`, '%Y-%m-%d %H:%i:%s'), 'Pending'),
       CASE WHEN o.`Paid Date` IS NULL THEN 'Unpaid' ELSE 'Paid' END, os.`Status Name`
FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.ID = o.`Customer ID` LEFT JOIN shippers sh ON sh.ID = o.`Shipper ID` LEFT JOIN `orders status` os ON os.`Status ID` = o.`Status ID`
WHERE NOT (o.`Status ID` = 3) ORDER BY o.`Order ID`;
entries.explanation: IFNULL(x, default) replaces NULL; IF(cond, a, b) is the inline conditional. LEFT JOINs keep orders with a missing shipper. Note `Status ID` <> 3 silently drops orders whose Status ID is NULL (none in this dump).
mistakes: INNER JOIN shippers (drops unassigned orders).
Status ID <> 3 with NULL statuses.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q30
entries.question: Using conditional aggregation, produce one row per employee with the employee's full name, the total number of orders, and one column per order status (New, Invoiced, Shipped, Closed) holding the number of orders in that status. Add a column with the percentage of the employee's orders that are Closed (1 decimal). Include employees with no orders. Sort by total orders descending, then name.
entries.answer:
SELECT CONCAT(e.`First Name`, ' ', e.`Last Name`) AS full_name,
       COUNT(o.`Order ID`) AS total_orders,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN o.`Status ID` = 0 THEN 1 END) AS new_orders,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN o.`Status ID` = 1 THEN 1 END) AS invoiced,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN o.`Status ID` = 2 THEN 1 END) AS shipped,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN o.`Status ID` = 3 THEN 1 END) AS closed,
       COALESCE(ROUND(100 * COUNT(CASE WHEN o.`Status ID` = 3 THEN 1 END) / NULLIF(COUNT(o.`Order ID`), 0), 1), 0) AS pct_closed
FROM employees AS e
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.`Employee ID` = e.ID
GROUP BY e.ID, full_name
ORDER BY total_orders DESC, full_name;
entries.alternative:
SELECT CONCAT(e.`First Name`, ' ', e.`Last Name`) AS full_name,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.`Employee ID` = e.ID) AS total_orders,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.`Employee ID` = e.ID AND o.`Status ID` = 0),
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.`Employee ID` = e.ID AND o.`Status ID` = 1),
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.`Employee ID` = e.ID AND o.`Status ID` = 2),
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.`Employee ID` = e.ID AND o.`Status ID` = 3),
       COALESCE(ROUND(100 * (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.`Employee ID` = e.ID AND o.`Status ID` = 3) / NULLIF((SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.`Employee ID` = e.ID), 0), 1), 0)
FROM employees e ORDER BY total_orders DESC, full_name;
entries.explanation: COUNT(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 END) counts only matching rows and returns 0 (not NULL) for employees without orders; SUM(cond) would give NULL for them. NULLIF(..., 0) avoids division by zero, COALESCE turns the NULL percentage into 0. Status IDs: 0 New, 1 Invoiced, 2 Shipped, 3 Closed.
mistakes: SUM(CASE ... ) returns NULL for employees without orders.
COUNT(CASE ... ELSE 0 END) counts everything.
Division by zero giving NULL.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q31
entries.question: Report the top 5 customers by total sales value (Quantity * `Unit Price` * (1 - Discount)). For each, show the company, the city, the number of distinct orders, the total sales value (2 decimals), the dates of the first and last order formatted as 'YYYY-MM-DD', and a tier: 'Gold' for sales of at least 10000, 'Silver' for at least 3000, 'Bronze' otherwise. Explain why the number of orders must be counted with COUNT(DISTINCT ...).
entries.answer:
SELECT c.Company, c.City,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.`Order ID`) AS n_orders,
       ROUND(SUM(od.Quantity * od.`Unit Price` * (1 - od.Discount)), 2) AS total_sales,
       DATE_FORMAT(MIN(o.`Order Date`), '%Y-%m-%d') AS first_order,
       DATE_FORMAT(MAX(o.`Order Date`), '%Y-%m-%d') AS last_order,
       CASE WHEN SUM(od.Quantity * od.`Unit Price` * (1 - od.Discount)) >= 10000 THEN 'Gold'
            WHEN SUM(od.Quantity * od.`Unit Price` * (1 - od.Discount)) >= 3000 THEN 'Silver'
            ELSE 'Bronze' END AS tier
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o ON o.`Customer ID` = c.ID
JOIN `order details` AS od ON od.`Order ID` = o.`Order ID`
GROUP BY c.ID, c.Company, c.City
ORDER BY SUM(od.Quantity * od.`Unit Price` * (1 - od.Discount)) DESC, c.Company
LIMIT 5;
entries.alternative:
SELECT Company, City, n, ROUND(s, 2), DATE_FORMAT(d1, '%Y-%m-%d'), DATE_FORMAT(d2, '%Y-%m-%d'), CASE WHEN s >= 10000 THEN 'Gold' WHEN s >= 3000 THEN 'Silver' ELSE 'Bronze' END
FROM (SELECT c.ID, c.Company, c.City, COUNT(DISTINCT o.`Order ID`) AS n, SUM(od.Quantity * od.`Unit Price` * (1 - od.Discount)) AS s, MIN(o.`Order Date`) AS d1, MAX(o.`Order Date`) AS d2
      FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.`Customer ID` = c.ID JOIN `order details` od ON od.`Order ID` = o.`Order ID` GROUP BY c.ID, c.Company, c.City) t
ORDER BY s DESC, Company LIMIT 5;
entries.explanation: After joining order details, each order appears once per line, so COUNT(*) or COUNT(o.`Order ID`) would count LINES; COUNT(DISTINCT o.`Order ID`) counts orders. The tier thresholds use the unrounded sum.
mistakes: COUNT(*) instead of COUNT(DISTINCT ...) (fan-out).
Tier thresholds checked in the wrong order (Silver before Gold).

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q32
entries.question: Produce a category sales pivot for the first half of 2006: one row per product category that has sales, with one column per month from January to June holding the sales value of that month (rounded to 0 decimals), and a final column with the half-year total. Sort by the total, highest first.
entries.answer:
SELECT p.Category,
       COALESCE(ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN MONTH(o.`Order Date`) = 1 THEN od.Quantity * od.`Unit Price` * (1 - od.Discount) END), 0), 0) AS january,
       COALESCE(ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN MONTH(o.`Order Date`) = 2 THEN od.Quantity * od.`Unit Price` * (1 - od.Discount) END), 0), 0) AS february,
       COALESCE(ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN MONTH(o.`Order Date`) = 3 THEN od.Quantity * od.`Unit Price` * (1 - od.Discount) END), 0), 0) AS march,
       COALESCE(ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN MONTH(o.`Order Date`) = 4 THEN od.Quantity * od.`Unit Price` * (1 - od.Discount) END), 0), 0) AS april,
       COALESCE(ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN MONTH(o.`Order Date`) = 5 THEN od.Quantity * od.`Unit Price` * (1 - od.Discount) END), 0), 0) AS may,
       COALESCE(ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN MONTH(o.`Order Date`) = 6 THEN od.Quantity * od.`Unit Price` * (1 - od.Discount) END), 0), 0) AS june,
       ROUND(SUM(od.Quantity * od.`Unit Price` * (1 - od.Discount)), 0) AS half_year_total
FROM products AS p
JOIN `order details` AS od ON od.`Product ID` = p.ID
JOIN orders AS o ON o.`Order ID` = od.`Order ID`
WHERE o.`Order Date` >= '2006-01-01' AND o.`Order Date` < '2006-07-01'
GROUP BY p.Category
ORDER BY half_year_total DESC, p.Category;
entries.alternative:
SELECT Category,
       COALESCE(ROUND(SUM(IF(m = 1, v, NULL)), 0), 0), COALESCE(ROUND(SUM(IF(m = 2, v, NULL)), 0), 0), COALESCE(ROUND(SUM(IF(m = 3, v, NULL)), 0), 0),
       COALESCE(ROUND(SUM(IF(m = 4, v, NULL)), 0), 0), COALESCE(ROUND(SUM(IF(m = 5, v, NULL)), 0), 0), COALESCE(ROUND(SUM(IF(m = 6, v, NULL)), 0), 0),
       ROUND(SUM(v), 0) AS t
FROM (SELECT p.Category, MONTH(o.`Order Date`) AS m, od.Quantity * od.`Unit Price` * (1 - od.Discount) AS v
      FROM products p JOIN `order details` od ON od.`Product ID` = p.ID JOIN orders o ON o.`Order ID` = od.`Order ID`
      WHERE o.`Order Date` >= '2006-01-01' AND o.`Order Date` < '2006-07-01') x
GROUP BY Category ORDER BY t DESC, Category;
entries.explanation: Pivot = SUM(CASE WHEN month = n THEN value END) per month column; the WHERE keeps January-June 2006 (so MONTH() is unambiguous). COALESCE turns empty months into 0. The total is rounded from the exact sum, so it can differ by 1 from the sum of the rounded columns. Sales value = Quantity * `Unit Price` * (1 - Discount).
mistakes: MONTH() without limiting the year.
Rounding before summing.
Forgetting COALESCE for empty months.

entries.sourceRef: lab/Northwind_SQL_Lab.docx Q33
entries.question: Build a stock report from `inventory transactions`, where `Transaction Type` 1 = Purchased (adds stock), 2 = Sold, 3 = On Hold and 4 = Waste (the last three remove stock). For every product that has at least one transaction, show the product name, the units purchased, sold and on hold, the stock on hand (purchased minus everything removed), the Reorder Level, and an action column: 'Reorder' when stock on hand is at or below the reorder level, 'OK' otherwise. List the 'Reorder' products first; within each action, sort by stock on hand and then product name.
entries.answer:
SELECT t.`Product Name`, t.purchased, t.sold, t.on_hold, t.stock_on_hand, t.`Reorder Level`,
       CASE WHEN t.stock_on_hand <= t.`Reorder Level` THEN 'Reorder' ELSE 'OK' END AS action
FROM (SELECT p.ID, p.`Product Name`, p.`Reorder Level`,
             SUM(CASE WHEN it.`Transaction Type` = 1 THEN it.Quantity ELSE 0 END) AS purchased,
             SUM(CASE WHEN it.`Transaction Type` = 2 THEN it.Quantity ELSE 0 END) AS sold,
             SUM(CASE WHEN it.`Transaction Type` = 3 THEN it.Quantity ELSE 0 END) AS on_hold,
             SUM(CASE WHEN it.`Transaction Type` = 1 THEN it.Quantity ELSE -it.Quantity END) AS stock_on_hand
      FROM products AS p
      JOIN `inventory transactions` AS it ON it.`Product ID` = p.ID
      GROUP BY p.ID, p.`Product Name`, p.`Reorder Level`) AS t
ORDER BY FIELD(CASE WHEN t.stock_on_hand <= t.`Reorder Level` THEN 'Reorder' ELSE 'OK' END, 'Reorder', 'OK'), t.stock_on_hand, t.`Product Name`;
entries.alternative:
SELECT p.`Product Name`,
       SUM(it.Quantity * (it.`Transaction Type` = 1)), SUM(it.Quantity * (it.`Transaction Type` = 2)), SUM(it.Quantity * (it.`Transaction Type` = 3)),
       SUM(it.Quantity * IF(it.`Transaction Type` = 1, 1, -1)), p.`Reorder Level`,
       IF(SUM(it.Quantity * IF(it.`Transaction Type` = 1, 1, -1)) <= p.`Reorder Level`, 'Reorder', 'OK')
FROM products p JOIN `inventory transactions` it ON it.`Product ID` = p.ID
GROUP BY p.ID, p.`Product Name`, p.`Reorder Level`
ORDER BY IF(SUM(it.Quantity * IF(it.`Transaction Type` = 1, 1, -1)) <= p.`Reorder Level`, 0, 1), SUM(it.Quantity * IF(it.`Transaction Type` = 1, 1, -1)), p.`Product Name`;
entries.explanation: Types: 1 Purchased (+), 2 Sold, 3 On Hold, 4 Waste (all three subtract). Conditional SUM per type; stock = purchased minus everything removed. A SELECT alias cannot be reused in the same SELECT, hence the derived table. INNER JOIN keeps products with at least one transaction. The ORDER BY puts 'Reorder' first.
mistakes: Status column does not exist: use `Transaction Type`.
Using the alias stock_on_hand in the same SELECT list.
Adding On Hold stock instead of subtracting.

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_3.png Q4 (1p) - question text transcribed from the image

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_3.png Q5 (1p) - question text transcribed from the image
entries.question: List the products with their Product Name, Category, List Price, and Standard Cost. Items are sorted by List Price and Standard Cost from the most expensive.

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_3.png Q6 (1p) - question text transcribed from the image
entries.question: List products whose categories are Pasta, Soups, or Beverages and List Price is greater than $10, sorting the name alphabetically.
entries.answer:

FROM products
WHERE Category IN ('Pasta', 'Soups', 'Beverages')
  AND `List Price` > 10
ORDER BY `Product Name`;

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_3.png Q7 (1p) - question text transcribed from the image

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_3.png Q8 (1p) - question text transcribed from the image
entries.question: Find Orders having Payment Type equal to "Credit Card"

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_3.png Q9 (1p) - question text transcribed from the image
entries.question: Show the 10 latest Purchase Orders
entries.answer:
SELECT *
FROM `purchase orders`
ORDER BY `Creation Date` DESC, `Purchase Order ID` DESC
LIMIT 10;
entries.alternative:
SELECT `Purchase Order ID`, `Supplier ID`, `Created By`, `Submitted Date`, `Creation Date`, `Status ID`, `Expected Date`, `Shipping Fee`, `Taxes`, `Payment Date`, `Payment Amount`, `Payment Method`, `Notes`, `Approved By`, `Approved Date`, `Submitted By`
FROM (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY `Creation Date` DESC, `Purchase Order ID` DESC) AS rn FROM `purchase orders`) t WHERE rn <= 10 ORDER BY rn;
entries.explanation: 'Latest' is interpreted as most recently CREATED (`Creation Date`); use `Submitted Date` if the course means submission. DESC + LIMIT 10 returns the newest rows.
mistakes: ORDER BY without DESC (oldest first).
LIMIT without ORDER BY.

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_3.png Q10 (1p) - question text transcribed from the image
entries.question: Find Orders being shipped in March.

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_3.png Q11 (1p) - question text transcribed from the image
entries.question: Compute the value of each line of table Order Details. The results should have two columns: OrderDetailID, and Value where Value = (Quantity * [Unit Price])*(1-Discount)

SELECT ID AS OrderDetailID, (Quantity * `Unit Price`) * (1 - Discount) AS Value
FROM `order details`;
entries.alternative: SELECT od.ID, (od.Quantity * od.`Unit Price`) * (1 - od.Discount) FROM `order details` od;
entries.explanation: Expression in the SELECT list with an alias; `order details` needs backticks. This line value is reused in later questions (Assignment 4 Q12, Q15).

Missing backticks on `Unit Price`.

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_3.png Q12 (1p) - question text transcribed from the image

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_3.png Q13 (1p) - question text transcribed from the image
entries.question: Compute how many purchase orders have been approved in the year 2006.

BETWEEN with the last day at 00:00:00.

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_3.png Q14 (1p) - question text transcribed from the image
entries.question: Compute the total shipping fee of all orders in June

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_3.png Q15 (2p) - question text transcribed from the image

FROM customers

LIKE 'Manager' without wildcards.

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_3.png Q16 (2p) - question text transcribed from the image
entries.question: Show the list of Employees with 3 columns as in the bellow picture, whereas the column Full Name is the combination of First Name and Last Name and the Last Name are in upper case.
entries.answer:
SELECT CONCAT(`First Name`, ' ', UPPER(`Last Name`)) AS `Full Name`, `E-mail Address`, `Job Title`
FROM employees;

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_3.png Q17 (2p) - question text transcribed from the image
entries.question: Note that in table Products, all product names have the prefix "Northwind Traders". Show the products' names in a short format without that prefix as in the below picture.

SELECT REPLACE(`Product Name`, 'Northwind Traders ', '') AS `Short Product Name`

mistakes: Forgetting the trailing space (leaves a leading blank).

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_4_1.png + asg_4_2.png Q1 - question text transcribed from the images
entries.question: Show the product (all columns) whose deviation between List Price and Standard Cost is the largest.
entries.alternative: SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY ABS(`List Price` - `Standard Cost`) DESC LIMIT 1;
entries.explanation: 'Deviation' is read as the absolute difference. The MAX subquery keeps ties; ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 returns one row only. If the course means a ratio/percentage, change the expression.
mistakes: Largest List Price - Standard Cost without ABS.
Aggregate in WHERE without a subquery.

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_4_1.png + asg_4_2.png Q2 - question text transcribed from the images
entries.question: Show the best seller product(s) (which is one being ordered the most so far)
entries.answer:
SELECT p.ID, p.`Product Name`, SUM(od.Quantity) AS total_quantity
FROM products AS p
JOIN `order details` AS od ON od.`Product ID` = p.ID
GROUP BY p.ID, p.`Product Name`
HAVING SUM(od.Quantity) = (SELECT MAX(t.q) FROM (SELECT SUM(Quantity) AS q FROM `order details` GROUP BY `Product ID`) AS t);
entries.alternative: SELECT ID, `Product Name`, q FROM (SELECT p.ID, p.`Product Name`, SUM(od.Quantity) AS q, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(od.Quantity) DESC) AS rk FROM products p JOIN `order details` od ON od.`Product ID` = p.ID GROUP BY p.ID, p.`Product Name`) x WHERE rk = 1;
entries.explanation: 'Ordered the most' is read as the largest total QUANTITY (count order lines instead if the course means frequency). HAVING compares with the maximum so ties are all returned.
mistakes: LIMIT 1 hides ties.
COUNT(*) of lines instead of SUM(Quantity).

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_4_1.png + asg_4_2.png Q3 - question text transcribed from the images
entries.question: Compute the average List Price of all products
entries.answer:
SELECT AVG(`List Price`) AS avg_list_price
FROM products;
entries.alternative: SELECT SUM(`List Price`) / COUNT(`List Price`) FROM products;
entries.explanation: AVG ignores NULLs.

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_4_1.png + asg_4_2.png Q4 - question text transcribed from the images
entries.question: Compute the average List Price and the standard deviation of each category
entries.alternative:
SELECT Category, ROUND(AVG(`List Price`), 2), ROUND(SQRT(AVG(POW(`List Price` - m, 2))), 4)
FROM (SELECT p.*, AVG(p.`List Price`) OVER (PARTITION BY p.Category) AS m FROM products p) t GROUP BY Category;
entries.explanation: STDDEV = STDDEV_POP (population, MySQL default); use STDDEV_SAMP for the sample standard deviation (NULL for categories with a single product). ROUND is added only for readable output.
mistakes: STDDEV_SAMP gives NULL for one-product categories.

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_4_1.png + asg_4_2.png Q12 - question text transcribed from the images
entries.question: Compute the subtotal of each Order ID where the subtotal is the sum of values of all the corresponding order lines. Note: the value of each line was mentioned in question 11 of Assignment 3, which is (Quantity * [Unit Price])*(1-Discount)

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_4_1.png + asg_4_2.png Q13 - question text transcribed from the images
entries.question: Show the Order ID(s) with a subtotal greater than 1500 in the descending order.
entries.answer:
SELECT `Order ID`, SUM((Quantity * `Unit Price`) * (1 - Discount)) AS subtotal
FROM `order details`
GROUP BY `Order ID`
HAVING SUM((Quantity * `Unit Price`) * (1 - Discount)) > 1500
ORDER BY subtotal DESC, `Order ID`;

entries.sourceRef: lab/asg_4_1.png + asg_4_2.png Q14 - question text transcribed from the images
entries.question: Count how many orders each Employee ID have processed. If an Employee ID has no corresponding order, his results should be 0. A part of the results will look like the below figure.
entries.answer:
SELECT e.ID AS Employee, COUNT(o.`Order ID`) AS No_Orders
FROM employees AS e
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.`Employee ID` = e.ID
GROUP BY e.ID;
entries.alternative: SELECT e.ID, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.`Employee ID` = e.ID) FROM employees e;
entries.explanation: LEFT JOIN + COUNT(o.`Order ID`) gives 0 for employees without orders. The values drawn in the exercise figure do not have to match this dump: compare with your own query result, not the picture.
